name: Courvoisier's Law
statement: A painless, palpably enlarged gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to gallstones.
statementAccent: unlikely to be due to gallstones
meaning: In a jaundiced patient, a gallbladder that is enlarged enough to feel but does not hurt points away from gallstone disease and toward obstruction of the bile duct by malignancy, such as cancer of the pancreatic head or the bile duct. It is a bedside rule of thumb for narrowing the cause of obstructive jaundice, not a diagnosis in itself.
mechanism: Chronic gallstone disease scars and thickens the gallbladder wall through repeated inflammation, leaving it fibrotic and unable to distend, and the process is typically painful. A slow-growing malignant obstruction instead blocks the common bile duct downstream of a previously healthy gallbladder, letting back-pressure distend it smoothly and painlessly.

examples.text: A tumor of the pancreatic head gradually occludes the common bile duct, producing painless jaundice with a distended, palpable gallbladder.
A distal bile duct cancer causes slow obstruction and a non-tender palpable gallbladder, consistent with the rule.
A gallstone lodged in the common bile duct alongside one blocking the cystic duct can produce a palpable, non-tender gallbladder, violating the rule.

whyItMatters: It gives clinicians a fast, no-cost bedside heuristic to prioritize suspicion of pancreatic or biliary malignancy in a jaundiced patient. That early suspicion drives appropriate imaging and referral before laboratory or scan results return.
limits: It is a probabilistic tendency, not an absolute law, and both false positives and false negatives occur. Some patients with malignant obstruction never develop a palpable gallbladder, and rare stone combinations can mimic the classic picture. Modern imaging has largely superseded reliance on the sign.
misreadings: Courvoisier's original 1890 report described common-duct obstruction and did not itself state a "law" or explicitly name malignancy or painlessness; the familiar wording accreted afterward and is often misquoted.
origin: Ludwig Georg Courvoisier, Swiss surgeon, from observations published in 1890.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on Courvoisier's law, giving the modern statement, the attribution to Courvoisier (1890), and the fibrosis-versus-malignancy mechanism — supports the statement, origin, and mechanism.
Verghese A, Dison C, Berk SL, "Courvoisier's 'law' — an eponym in evolution," American Journal of Gastroenterology, 1987 — supports that the eponym evolved over time and is frequently misquoted.
